Standard KJV text as reprinted today (Project Gutenberg eBook #10)

source.excerpt: Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding. He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
trail: Project Gutenberg eBook #10, The King James Version of the Bible ↗ gives Isaiah 40:31 exactly as quoted: “But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles…”
Wikisource’s King James Bible, Isaiah ↗ carries the same verse word for word at chapter 40, verse 31.

Wikipedia on the King James Version ↗: published by Robert Barker, the King’s Printer, in 1611. Benjamin Blayney’s 1769 Oxford edition became the standard text, “reproduced almost unchanged in most current printings.”
Wikipedia on Isaiah 40 ↗ describes the chapter as the first of the section known as Deutero-Isaiah (Isaiah 40–55), dated to the Israelites’ exile in Babylon.
source.excerptNote: Verses 28–31 from the King James Version. The popular quotation is verse 31 alone, word for word. A search of Quote Investigator and Wikiquote found no investigation of this line, and there is no rival claimant to its authorship.
source.rightsNote: The English wording is the King James Version, first published in 1611, long before the 1931 cutoff, so it is in the public domain in the United States. Wikipedia notes one exception: the KJV is “perpetually copyrighted in UK” and de facto public domain elsewhere (Wikipedia ↗). Modern translations of the same verse, such as the NIV or ESV, are separate works and may be under copyright.

author.name: The Book of Isaiah
author.heading: About the Book of Isaiah
author.metaLine: Hebrew Bible prophetic book · chapters 40–55 dated by most scholars to the Babylonian exile (6th century BCE)
author.bio: The Book of Isaiah opens with a heading naming its words as those of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz, who is dated to the 8th century BCE. Through most of the 20th century the scholarly consensus was that he did not write the whole book. That view splits it into three collections. Chapters 40–55, known as Deutero-Isaiah, are “the work of an anonymous author writing during the Exile in the 6th century BCE.” Recent research has challenged the three-part view and stresses the book’s unity (Wikipedia ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The verse closes Isaiah chapter 40. Most scholars treat that chapter as the opening of Deutero-Isaiah, the part of the book addressed to the Israelites in exile in Babylon (Wikipedia ↗). It answers a complaint voiced a few lines earlier: “My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God” (40:27).

The reply runs from a God who “fainteth not, neither is weary,” to the people: even the young will stumble, but those who wait on the LORD will be renewed. The run-without-weariness image is why the verse turns up so often on cards, plaques and athletic banners. In the King James Version, “LORD” in capitals marks where the Hebrew uses the divine name.
